reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A thin mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction of the distal oesophagus, at the top of a hiatus hernia when present
Classically causes intermittent dysphagia to solids, often with abrupt food impaction after bolting food or drinking alcohol ('steakhouse syndrome')
Symptoms typically appear when the luminal diameter narrows below a critical threshold
Best seen on a barium swallow with the oesophagus fully distended, as it can be overlooked at endoscopy
Frequently coexists with a hiatus hernia and with gastro-oesophageal reflux, which may contribute to its formation
Symptomatic rings are treated by endoscopic dilatation, and coexisting reflux is addressed to reduce recurrence
Distinguished from a proximal web by its location at the gastro-oesophageal junction and its circumferential shape
reference.pathophysiology: A Schatzki ring is a circumferential mucosal ring at the gastro-oesophageal junction, with squamous epithelium above and columnar epithelium below. Its exact cause is debated, but chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux and mechanical factors are implicated in its development and in progressive narrowing. The ring reduces the maximal luminal diameter, so large solid boluses intermittently lodge above it, producing episodic dysphagia and, when a bolus fully obstructs the lumen, acute food impaction.
additionalDifferentials: Muscular (A) ring of the lower oesophagus
additionalInvestigations: Barium swallow with full oesophageal distension and a solid bolus challenge
Upper endoscopy for confirmation, biopsy, and dilatation
Oesophageal biopsies to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis
Ambulatory reflux monitoring where reflux contribution is uncertain
redFlags: Progressive dysphagia or weight loss suggesting stricture or malignancy
Acute food impaction requiring urgent endoscopy
Recurrent rings that may indicate untreated reflux or eosinophilic oesophagitis
reference.prognosis: Dilatation of a symptomatic ring is usually effective and safe, though rings can recur; addressing coexisting reflux may reduce the recurrence rate.
pitfalls: Missing the ring at endoscopy because the oesophagus is inadequately distended
Overlooking eosinophilic oesophagitis as a cause of recurrent rings and dysphagia
Failing to treat coexisting reflux, allowing the ring to recur
Attributing solid-food dysphagia to a ring without excluding malignancy
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Treat a symptomatic ring with endoscopic dilatation to widen the luminal diameter and relieve dysphagia
Relieve acute food bolus impaction by endoscopic disimpaction
Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor to control coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux and reduce the risk of recurrence
Exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis with oesophageal biopsies before attributing dysphagia solely to the ring
Advise careful eating, thorough chewing, and avoiding large boluses and alcohol-associated bolting of food
Repeat dilatation for symptomatic recurrence, as rings may re-form over time
